sentences.text: Lucianovenator is an extinct coelophysoid theropod dinosaur distinguished by a unique combination of four specific pairs of paired pits on its cervical vertebrae.

Its anterior cervical ribs are exceptionally long, measuring more than five times the length of the vertebrae, while the edge of each centrodiapophyseal lamina develops a long, deep pit that grows progressively longer and deeper toward the base of the neck.
The genus name Lucianovenator means "Luciano's hunter" and honors Don Luciano Leyes, who first reported the fossil remains, and the genus was formally named by Martinez and Apaldetti in 2017.
The holotype specimen PVSJ 906 was discovered in 2014 by paleontologist Ricardo N. Martínez and his team at the Universidad Nacional de San Juan within the Quebrada del Barro Formation in Argentina.

This holotype consists of an articulated sequence of vertebrae from the third cervical to the fourth dorsal, along with a sacrum and a partial pelvis, while three additional specimens and a proximal right tibia have been referred to the species.
There is currently only one recorded fossil occurrence of Lucianovenator.
Lucianovenator is one of the few known neotheropod dinosaurs from South America.

An initial phylogenetic analysis placed Lucianovenator in the family Coelophysidae alongside Coelophysis rhodesiensis and Camposaurus, but later phylogenetic studies recovered Lucianovenator as a coelophysoid that is not a member of the Coelophysidae family.
The initial clade grouping Lucianovenator with other dinosaurs was supported by the single feature of fused sacral zygapophyses.
The fossils date to the late Norian to Rhaetian stages, approximately 210 to 202 million years ago, though the Norian stage is specifically defined as between 227.3 and 205.7 million years ago.

While the genus Lucianovenator belongs to the family Coelophysidae according to some classifications, later studies suggest it is a coelophysoid outside that family, creating ongoing debate about its exact placement.
